title: Retry 1 · Q1 · from M2 Q23
body:
Information ratio (IR): Candidate A 0.700; B 0.630; C 0.540.
Transfer coefficient: 0.70; 0.60; 0.45. Information coefficient: 0.10; 0.15; 0.20. Number of securities: 100; 49; 36.

questions.q: Based on the data, the candidate with the greatest skill at achieving active returns appears to be:
questions.why: The IR measures the consistency of active return per unit of active risk; the highest IR means the most skill. A = 0.70 × 0.10 × √100 = 0.700; B = 0.60 × 0.15 × √49 = 0.630; C = 0.45 × 0.20 × √36 = 0.540. Candidate C has the highest IC but low breadth and TC pull its IR down.

body: A manager states that the carry arbitrage model assumes: (1) transaction costs are negligible; (2) short-sale proceeds are available immediately; (3) the borrowing rate may be higher than the lending rate.

title: Retry 1 · Q4 · from M2 Q15
body:
Stock price $50; call strike $48; risk-free rate 3%; up factor 1.25; down factor 0.80; no dividend. The one-year call trades at $6.60.
Strategy 1: sell the call and buy shares using borrowed funds. Strategy 2: buy the call, short-sell shares and lend the proceeds. Strategy 3: buy the call using borrowed funds.

questions.q: With respect to the one-year call option, which strategy is most likely correct?
questions.why: One-year model value = π × (S·u − K) ÷ (1 + r) = 0.5111 × 14.5 ÷ 1.03 = $7.20, above the market price $6.60: the call is underpriced. Buy the call and sell the replicating portfolio (short shares and lend): Strategy 2. Selling the call is the wrong side, and buying it with borrowed funds adds risk instead of locking in the gain.

title: Retry 1 · Q5 · from M2 Q20
body: A bond's near-term credit spreads are below its longer-term credit spreads: the credit spread curve is upward sloping.

questions.q: The upward-sloping credit spread curve is most likely due to:
options: strong current cash flow and high profit margins.
market expectations of improved future profitability.
a relatively stable expectation of default over time.
questions.why: An upward-sloping credit curve is characteristic of a high-quality issuer with strong current cash flow and margins. A stable default expectation gives a flat curve; improving expectations after distress give an inverted curve.

title: Retry 1 · Q7 · from M1 Q32
body: An intern says: "Adjusted R² is more appropriate than R² for a model with several independent variables because it is adjusted for degrees of freedom; adjusted R² can never be negative."

questions.q: The intern's statement is:
options: incorrect with regard to adjusted R² never being negative.
incorrect with regard to its appropriateness for a multiple regression.
questions.why: Adjusted R² is the better measure with several variables, so that part is right. But adjusted R² CAN be negative (when R² is low and k is large relative to n); plain R² cannot. One wrong part makes the whole statement incorrect.

body:
Service cost 310; past service cost 120.
Discount rate on liabilities 6.0%; benefit obligation at beginning of year 48,000.
Plan assets at beginning of year 44,000; expected rate of return on plan assets 7.0%.
Assume the actuarial loss is not immediately recognized and there is no amortization of past service costs or actuarial gains and losses.

questions.q: If the company prepared its financial statements under US GAAP, the total amount recognized on its income statement related to the defined benefit plan for the year is closest to:
questions.why: US GAAP P&L cost = service cost + interest cost − expected return = 310 + 2,880 − 3,080 = 110. Past service cost goes to OCI and is not amortized here, so adding it (230) is wrong. 670 is the IFRS-type figure: service + past service + net interest (240).

title: Retry 1 · Q12 · from M1 Q44
body:
Current portfolio standard deviation 9.00%. The variance of the combined portfolio must be less than 85% of the current portfolio's variance; maximize risk-adjusted return with large negative events expected.
Standard deviation / Sortino ratio: merger arbitrage 8.10% / 1.45; systematic futures 8.60% / 1.80; equity market neutral 7.70% / 1.60.

questions.q: Which simulated portfolio is most suitable?
questions.why: Maximum variance = 0.85 × 9.00² = 68.85, so maximum SD = 8.30%. Systematic futures (8.60%) fails. Merger arbitrage (8.10%) and equity market neutral (7.70%) pass. With large negative events expected, use the Sortino ratio: 1.60 > 1.45, so equity market neutral.

Weighted average expected volatility used to value option grants: 25.00% for 2024 grants; 22.00% for 2023 grants.
Higher volatility raises an option's fair value.

questions.q: If the company had used for its 2024 option grants the same volatility assumption it used for 2023, its 2024 net income would have been:
questions.why: Using the 2023 volatility (22%) instead of 25% lowers the fair value of the 2024 options. A lower fair value means a lower compensation expense, so net income would have been higher.

title: Retry 1 · Q14 · from M1 Q43
body: A hedge fund adviser wants a specialist strategy that lets the fund maintain a high Sharpe ratio even during a financial crisis when equity markets fall.

questions.q: The specialist strategy that fits this objective is most likely:
options: buying longer-dated out-of-the-money options on VIX index futures.
selling equity volatility and collecting the volatility risk premium.
cross-asset volatility trading between two markets.
questions.why: Long volatility gains when equities fall (volatility is strongly negatively correlated with equity returns), so buying OTM VIX options protects in a crisis. Selling volatility loses in a crisis, and cross-asset volatility trading carries idiosyncratic macro risk.

body: A firm proposes these procedures for allocating block trades. Recommendation 1: partially filled block orders are allocated pro rata to the participating accounts. Recommendation 2: block trades are allocated first to the accounts that pay the firm the highest fees.

questions.q: Are the recommendations most likely consistent with the CFA Institute Recommended Procedures for Compliance with Standard III(B): Fair Dealing?
questions.why: Pro rata allocation of partial fills is a recommended fair-dealing procedure. Favoring accounts that pay higher fees treats clients unfairly and violates III(B).

Market price KRW48,000 per share; shares outstanding 25,000,000; total equity 640,000 (KRW millions); net income 96,500 (KRW millions).

questions.why: Justified P/B = (ROE − g) ÷ (r − g) = (0.14 − 0.06) ÷ (0.10 − 0.06) = 2.00. 1.88 is the current market price ÷ book value per share (48,000 ÷ 25,600); 2.27 uses last year's ROE (15.08%).

title: Retry 1 · Q23 · from M1 Q24
body:
Country B consistently runs a current account deficit.
An analyst asserts, using the flow supply/demand channel, that Country B's currency should depreciate over time.

questions.q: The analyst's assertion is most likely:
options: correct because countries with persistent current account deficits tend to see their currencies depreciate.
incorrect because deficits are financed by borrowing, which makes the currency appreciate.
incorrect because the flow supply/demand channel applies only to countries with surpluses.
questions.why: The flow supply/demand channel says persistent surpluses lead to appreciation and persistent deficits lead to depreciation. The assertion is therefore correct. The channel applies to both surpluses and deficits, and borrowing to finance a deficit does not make the currency appreciate.

title: Retry 1 · Q24 · from M2 Q30
body:
Par curve (bonds priced at par, annual coupons): 1 year 2.0%; 2 years 3.6%; 3 years 5.5%.
A three-year 6% annual coupon corporate bond has a market price of 106.00.
Value the bond by discounting each cash flow separately with the appropriate spot rate.

questions.q: The amount (in absolute terms) by which the bond is mispriced is closest to:
questions.why: Bootstrap spot rates: z1 = 2.0%; z2 = 3.6293%; z3 = 5.6409%. Value = 101.3799; mispricing = 106.00 − 101.3799 = 4.62. Discounting with the par yields gives 101.7437 (mispricing 4.26); 6.00 is just price − par.
